intro: Welcome to grammar for style! You can already build clefts, inversion and fronting. Now you learn to choose: where the focus of a sentence should fall, which structure puts it there in a speech, an op-ed, a report or a LinkedIn post, and how varying sentence length gives your writing rhythm.
teachingNotes: Recap in one line each, don't re-teach. From c1-cleft-sentences: clefts move the spotlight (What I need is more time; It was Sari who called; All I want is…). From c1-inversion: a negative/limiting opener puts the auxiliary before the subject (Never have I seen…; Rarely do we…; Only when… did I…; Not only did…), plus Had I known / Should you need, and inversion is never required. From c1-emphasis-fronting: emphatic do, fronting (Much as I like it, …; Tired as she was, …; The salary I can accept; the hours I can't) and Such was the demand that…. The C2 step is CHOOSING, not forming.

Objective choose-for-focus: end-focus (new/important information at the end of the clause, where the main stress falls in speech), end-weight (long, heavy parts last: It surprised everyone that the ministry approved the budget… rather than a 15-word subject), and given-before-new across sentences (start with what the reader knows: this/these + a known word, the passive, a fronted linking phrase). The passive is chosen for linking or when the agent doesn't matter, not because it is 'more formal'. Indonesian traps: long yang-subjects translated word for word; every di- turned into a passive, or the passive avoided completely; topic + comma openings (Aplikasi itu, tiga mahasiswa yang membuatnya) that English writing doesn't use.

Objective inversion-cleft-fronting: match the tool to the job. Correcting an assumption → it-cleft (It isn't X that…; it's Y). Building to a climax in a speech → what-cleft or inversion, then a short sentence. Sharp contrast → fronting (The budget we can fix; trust we can't). Linking → passive or this/these. Plain order is better most of the time: one strong structure per paragraph; three in a row sound theatrical, especially on LinkedIn, in emails or chats. Accuracy is part of control; the node's common errors: *Never I have seen such a mess → Never have I seen; *Only when I read the report I understood the problem → …did I understand (inversion in the second part); *What I need it is more time → What I need is (adalah = is, no it).

Objective vary-sentences: explain simple (one clause), compound (two main clauses with and/but/so/or) and complex (main + dependent clause with when/because/although/which/if) in plain Indonesian. Habits: a short sentence after long ones for punch; mix the types (all short = choppy, all long = tiring); vary openings (subject, time phrase, dependent clause, participle clause); read aloud. Indonesian trap: formal Indonesian chains clauses with yang/dan/sehingga/serta into very long sentences; the opposite classroom habit is a row of 'We… We… We…' sentences.

Testing and honesty: at C2 these are style choices, so only test clear cases: form errors (missing or wrong auxiliary, extra it), which part is given vs new when the context states it, which structure fits a stated job (correcting an assumption → cleft; given first + new last → passive), and which revision fixes a clearly monotonous paragraph. Alternatives that are grammatical but put the focus on the wrong part are 'worse fits', not 'wrong': say so in feedback. Typed answers are normalised (punctuation removed). Contexts: a company anniversary speech, an op-ed, a report conclusion, a LinkedIn post; Jakarta, Bandung, Surabaya, Makassar, ministries, NGOs, startups.

Limits: no new forms. Don't teach locative inversion (On the table lay a letter; Here comes the bus) or so/such inversion beyond recognising them; no detailed theme/rheme terminology beyond given/new; no punctuation lessons (semicolons appear in examples only). Use original practice texts only; never quote real speeches, columns or literature beyond a few words.

keyPoints.title: End-focus, end-weight and given → new
keyPoints.explanation: English puts the new or most important information at the end of a sentence (end-focus) and long, heavy parts last (end-weight): It surprised everyone that the ministry approved the budget so quickly, rather than a long subject first. Across sentences, start with what the reader already knows (given) and end with what's new; this/these + a known word, the passive and fronted linking phrases help. The passive here isn't 'more formal': it's the order that links.

examples.en: The new office opens in Surabaya in March.
examples.id: Kantor baru di Surabaya dibuka bulan Maret.

examples.en: It surprised everyone that the ministry approved the budget without any discussion.
examples.id: Semua orang terkejut bahwa kementerian menyetujui anggaran itu tanpa diskusi sama sekali.

examples.en: The app was built by three students from Hasanuddin University.
examples.id: Aplikasi itu dibuat oleh tiga mahasiswa Universitas Hasanuddin.

id.title: End-focus, end-weight, dan yang lama → yang baru
id.explanation: Bahasa Inggris menaruh informasi yang baru atau paling penting di akhir kalimat (end-focus) dan bagian yang panjang dan berat di belakang (end-weight): It surprised everyone that the ministry approved the budget so quickly, bukan subjek panjang di depan. Antar kalimat, mulai dengan yang sudah diketahui pembaca (given) dan akhiri dengan yang baru; this/these + kata yang sudah dikenal, passive, dan frasa penghubung di depan membantu. Passive di sini bukan 'lebih formal': itu urutan yang menyambung.

keyPoints.title: Vary length, structure and openings
keyPoints.explanation: Mix simple sentences (one clause), compound sentences (two main clauses with and/but/so) and complex sentences (with when/because/although/which). Put a short sentence after long ones for punch, start sentences in different ways (a time phrase, a dependent clause, a participle clause) and read your paragraph aloud. All short sounds choppy; all long sounds tiring.

examples.en: When the budget was cut, the team found cheaper suppliers.
examples.id: Ketika anggarannya dipotong, tim itu menemukan pemasok yang lebih murah.

examples.en: Faced with these problems, we redesigned the app.
examples.id: Menghadapi masalah-masalah ini, kami mendesain ulang aplikasinya.

id.title: Variasikan panjang, struktur dan pembuka kalimat
id.explanation: Campur kalimat simple (satu klausa), compound (dua klausa utama dengan and/but/so) dan complex (dengan when/because/although/which). Taruh kalimat pendek setelah kalimat-kalimat panjang sebagai pukulan, mulai kalimat dengan cara berbeda (frasa waktu, anak kalimat, participle clause) dan bacakan paragrafmu dengan suara keras. Semuanya pendek terdengar patah-patah; semuanya panjang terdengar melelahkan.

keyPoints.title: Cleft, inversion, fronting: the right tool, used accurately
keyPoints.explanation: Use an it-cleft to correct an assumption (It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time), a what-cleft or inversion to build to a climax in a speech, fronting for a sharp contrast, and the passive to link. One strong structure per paragraph; plain order the rest of the time. Get the form right: Never have I seen (not Never I have), Only when I read it did I understand (inversion in the second part), What I need is (no extra it).

examples.en: It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time.
examples.id: Yang membuat klien kami khawatir bukan harganya, tapi waktu pengirimannya.

examples.en: Never before has our team grown so fast.
examples.id: Belum pernah tim kami tumbuh secepat ini.

examples.en: The budget we can fix; trust we can't.
examples.id: Anggaran bisa kita perbaiki; kepercayaan tidak.

id.title: Cleft, inversion, fronting: alat yang tepat, dipakai dengan akurat
id.explanation: Pakai it-cleft untuk meluruskan anggapan (It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time), what-cleft atau inversion untuk membangun puncak dalam pidato, fronting untuk kontras yang tajam, dan passive untuk menyambung. Satu struktur kuat per paragraf; selebihnya urutan biasa. Bentuknya harus benar: Never have I seen (bukan Never I have), Only when I read it did I understand (inversion di bagian kedua), What I need is (tanpa it tambahan).

expected: it surprised the donors that the project was finished two months early
guidedPractice.hint: It fills the subject slot; the long that-clause goes last (end-weight).

expected: never has our company had such a strong year
guidedPractice.hint: After Never at the start, the auxiliary (has) comes before the subject.

what i learned from my first startup was patience
guidedPractice.hint: What + clause + was + focus: no extra it (adalah = is/was).

assessment.prompt:
Speech at a company's 25th anniversary in Bandung. Write the missing auxiliary.
'Rarely ___ a small family workshop grown into a company with 2,000 employees. Tonight we celebrate the people who made it happen.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: has (negative opener Rarely → auxiliary before the subject; present perfect for a general truth up to now; a small family workshop is singular → has + grown). 'had' = 50 (correct inversion, but past perfect doesn't fit a statement about now). 'have' = 40 (inversion, but the subject is singular). 'did' or 'does' = 10 (grown needs has/had). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Report conclusion. Write the missing auxiliary.
'Only when the team compared the 2023 and 2024 data ___ they notice the pattern in the complaints.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: did (Only when + clause: the inversion is in the second part; past simple has no auxiliary, so did + base verb notice). 'do' = 30 (inversion, but the story is in the past). 'had' = 10 (had they notice is ungrammatical). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt:
This line from a LinkedIn post has one extra word that must be deleted. Write that word.
'What our industry needs it is fewer meetings and more honest feedback.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: it (a what-cleft is What + clause + is + focus; there is no extra it, from Indonesian 'Yang … adalah'). 'what' = 0 (What starts the cleft). 'is' = 0 (is is needed). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt: You're writing an op-ed about flooding in north Jakarta. Most readers assume heavy rain is the main cause. You want to correct that assumption and put the spotlight on the sinking land. Which structure from this list is made for that job: cleft, inversion, fronting, passive? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: cleft (an it-cleft corrects an assumption: It isn't the rain that…; it's the sinking land). 'what-cleft' = 80 (a cleft, though the it-cleft is the natural choice for correcting). 'passive' = 20 (it can move the cause to the end but doesn't correct the assumption). 'inversion' or 'fronting' = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Board meeting. A board member asks: 'And what's the biggest risk for the Surabaya project?'
You answer in one sentence with these three parts: the biggest risk · is · the timeline.
Following end-focus, which word comes last in your answer? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: timeline (The biggest risk is the timeline: 'the biggest risk' is given, it was in the question; 'the timeline' is the new answer, so it goes last). 'risk' = 20 (grammatical, The timeline is the biggest risk, but it ends on the known part). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Report conclusion (practice text). The paragraph is a row of short sentences: 'The budget was cut by 30 percent. The team still finished the project on time. The donors were impressed. …'
Combine the first two into one complex sentence. Write the missing word or words.
'___ the budget was cut by 30 percent, the team still finished the project on time.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: although / though / even though (a contrast clause makes a complex sentence; still confirms the contrast). 'while' / 'whilst' = 100 (contrast meaning). 'when' or 'after' = 50 (a complex sentence, but the contrast is lost). 'but' or 'despite' = 0 (but can't start this clause; despite needs a noun or -ing). Anything else = 0.

assessment.prompt:
Report conclusion. Sentence 1: 'In 2024 the ministry launched a reporting app for village health workers.'
In sentence 2 you want to start with the app (already known) and end with the new information: a team of four engineers from Surabaya. Which structure from this list does that: cleft, inversion, fronting, passive? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: passive (The app was built by a team of four engineers from Surabaya: given first, new last). 'cleft' = 20 (It was a team of four engineers who built the app focuses the team but can't start with the app). 'fronting' = 10 (The app a team of four engineers built ends on the verb, not the team). 'inversion' = 0.

material.title: The end of the sentence is the spotlight

blocks.text:
**Quick recap (C1):** you can already **form** these structures:
- **cleft** (kalimat yang dibelah dua): *What I need is more time. It was Sari who called.*
- **inversion** (kata kerja bantu pindah ke depan subjek): *Never have I seen such a mess. Only when I got home did I notice.*
- **fronting** (memindahkan satu bagian ke depan): *Much as I like it, I can't afford it. Such was the demand that…*
- the **passive**: *The app was designed by a team in Bandung.*
At C2 the question is no longer *how* to build them, but **which one this text needs, and when to leave them out**.
**Rule 1: end-focus** (fokus di akhir). English readers and listeners expect the **new or most important information at the end** of a sentence. In speech, the main stress usually falls there too. The same facts can carry different news, just by order:
- *The new office opens in March in **Surabaya**.* (the news is *where*)
- *The new office opens in Surabaya in **March**.* (the news is *when*)
**Rule 2: end-weight** (beban di akhir). Long, 'heavy' parts sound better **at the end**. A long subject at the start makes the reader wait a long time for the verb:
- *That the ministry approved the budget without any discussion surprised everyone.* (correct, but heavy)
- *It surprised everyone **that the ministry approved the budget without any discussion**.* (lighter)
You met this *It … that…* move in impersonal passives (*It is believed that…*): **it** fills the subject slot, and the heavy part waits at the end.
Honest note: these are tendencies of good style, not grammar rules. A sentence that breaks them is not wrong, just harder to read or aimed at the wrong point.

id.text:
**Rekap singkat (C1):** kamu sudah bisa **membentuk** struktur-struktur ini:
- **cleft** (kalimat yang dibelah dua): *What I need is more time. It was Sari who called.*
- **inversion** (kata kerja bantu pindah ke depan subjek): *Never have I seen such a mess. Only when I got home did I notice.*
- **fronting** (memindahkan satu bagian ke depan): *Much as I like it, I can't afford it. Such was the demand that…*
- **passive** (kalimat pasif, seperti di-): *The app was designed by a team in Bandung.*
Di C2 pertanyaannya bukan lagi *bagaimana* membentuknya, tapi **struktur mana yang dibutuhkan teks ini, dan kapan sebaiknya tidak dipakai**.
**Aturan 1: end-focus** (fokus di akhir). Pembaca dan pendengar bahasa Inggris mengharapkan **informasi yang baru atau paling penting ada di akhir** kalimat. Saat bicara, tekanan utama biasanya juga jatuh di situ. Fakta yang sama bisa membawa berita yang berbeda, hanya dengan urutan:
- *The new office opens in March in **Surabaya**.* (beritanya *di mana*)
- *The new office opens in Surabaya in **March**.* (beritanya *kapan*)
**Aturan 2: end-weight** (beban di akhir). Bagian yang panjang dan 'berat' terdengar lebih baik **di akhir**. Subjek yang panjang di awal membuat pembaca menunggu lama sebelum ketemu kata kerjanya:
- *That the ministry approved the budget without any discussion surprised everyone.* (benar, tapi berat)
- *It surprised everyone **that the ministry approved the budget without any discussion**.* (lebih ringan)
Kamu sudah bertemu gerakan *It … that…* ini di impersonal passive (*It is believed that…*): **it** mengisi tempat subjek, dan bagian yang berat menunggu di akhir.
Catatan jujur: ini kecenderungan gaya yang baik, bukan aturan grammar. Kalimat yang melanggarnya tidak salah, hanya lebih sulit dibaca atau menyorot hal yang keliru.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** formal Indonesian happily builds long subjects with *yang*: *Keputusan kementerian yang menyetujui anggaran tanpa diskusi itu mengejutkan semua orang.* Translated word for word, that gives a heavy English subject (*The decision of the ministry which approved the budget without any discussion surprised everyone*). It isn't wrong, but English readers prefer the heavy part **last**: *It surprised everyone that…*, or split it into two sentences.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia formal senang membuat subjek panjang dengan *yang*: *Keputusan kementerian yang menyetujui anggaran tanpa diskusi itu mengejutkan semua orang.* Kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata, hasilnya subjek bahasa Inggris yang berat (*The decision of the ministry which approved the budget without any discussion surprised everyone*). Ini tidak salah, tapi pembaca bahasa Inggris lebih suka bagian yang berat **di akhir**: *It surprised everyone that…*, atau pecah jadi dua kalimat.

blocks.prompt: A sentence for a report to the board. Which version follows end-weight better?
options: That three of our five suppliers in East Java may close next year worries the board.
It worries the board that three of our five suppliers in East Java may close next year.
blocks.explain: Both are grammatical, but the first makes the reader carry a 13-word subject before the verb. The second fills the subject slot with *it*, gets to the verb fast and puts the long, heavy part (and the news) at the end.

id.prompt: Kalimat untuk laporan ke dewan direksi. Versi mana yang lebih mengikuti end-weight?
id.explain: Keduanya benar secara grammar, tapi versi pertama membuat pembaca membawa subjek 13 kata sebelum ketemu kata kerjanya. Versi kedua mengisi tempat subjek dengan *it*, cepat sampai ke kata kerja, dan menaruh bagian yang panjang (dan beritanya) di akhir.

id.title: Yang lama dulu, baru yang baru: menyambung kalimat

blocks.text:
End-focus works **across sentences** too. Start each sentence with something the reader **already knows** (**given**: already mentioned or obvious) and end with something **new**. The new end of one sentence becomes the given start of the next, so the text flows like a chain:
- *Last year we launched a savings app for fishermen in Makassar. **The app** was built by **three students from Hasanuddin University**. **These students** now run a company with **twelve staff**.*
Tools that keep the given part first:
- **this / these / the + a word you've already used**: *This decision…, These figures…, The app…*
- **the passive**: *The app was built by three students…* The active *Three students built the app* is correct, but it puts the new information first and the known *the app* last.
- **fronting a linking phrase**: *Of these three options, the second is the cheapest.* (*Behind this decision was a long debate* is a different, more literary kind of inversion: you don't need it here.)
So the passive isn't 'weaker' or 'more formal' by itself: here it's simply **the order that links**.

id.text:
End-focus juga bekerja **antar kalimat**. Mulai setiap kalimat dengan sesuatu yang **sudah diketahui** pembaca (**given**: sudah disebut atau sudah jelas) dan akhiri dengan sesuatu yang **baru** (**new**). Bagian baru di akhir satu kalimat menjadi awal yang 'lama' di kalimat berikutnya, jadi teksnya mengalir seperti rantai:
- *Last year we launched a savings app for fishermen in Makassar. **The app** was built by **three students from Hasanuddin University**. **These students** now run a company with **twelve staff**.*
Alat untuk menjaga bagian yang lama tetap di depan:
- **this / these / the + kata yang sudah kamu pakai**: *This decision…, These figures…, The app…*
- **passive**: *The app was built by three students…* Versi aktif *Three students built the app* benar, tapi menaruh informasi baru di depan dan *the app* yang sudah diketahui di belakang.
- **frasa penghubung di depan (fronting)**: *Of these three options, the second is the cheapest.* (*Behind this decision was a long debate* adalah inversion jenis lain yang lebih sastrawi: kamu tidak membutuhkannya di sini.)
Jadi passive tidak otomatis 'lebih lemah' atau 'lebih formal': di sini passive hanyalah **urutan yang menyambung**.

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** Indonesian uses the *di-* passive all the time (*dibuat, dibangun, diresmikan*), so some learners turn every *di-* into an English passive. Others hear 'English prefers the active' and avoid the passive completely. Neither habit is the point. Ask: **which order puts the known part first and the news last?** Also, Indonesian can open with a topic and a comma (*Aplikasi itu, tiga mahasiswa yang membuatnya*). English doesn't do that in writing: use a passive or a cleft instead.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia memakai pasif *di-* terus-menerus (*dibuat, dibangun, diresmikan*), jadi sebagian pembelajar mengubah setiap *di-* menjadi passive bahasa Inggris. Yang lain mendengar 'bahasa Inggris lebih suka aktif' lalu menghindari passive sama sekali. Dua-duanya bukan intinya. Tanyakan: **urutan mana yang menaruh bagian yang sudah diketahui di depan dan beritanya di akhir?** Selain itu, bahasa Indonesia bisa dibuka dengan topik dan koma (*Aplikasi itu, tiga mahasiswa yang membuatnya*). Bahasa Inggris tulis tidak begitu: pakai passive atau cleft.

blocks.prompt: Previous sentence: 'In 2023 our NGO opened a small library in a village near Kupang.' Which sentence follows best?
options: The library now lends about 400 books a month.
About 400 books a month are now lent by the library.
Now lending about 400 books a month is the library.
blocks.explain: *The library* is given (just mentioned), so it goes first; the new fact, *400 books a month*, goes last. The second puts the new number first and the known library last. The third is an odd, theatrical inversion.

id.prompt: Kalimat sebelumnya: 'In 2023 our NGO opened a small library in a village near Kupang.' Kalimat mana yang paling cocok sebagai lanjutannya?
id.explain: *The library* sudah diketahui (baru saja disebut), jadi di depan; fakta barunya, *400 books a month*, di akhir. Pilihan kedua menaruh angka yang baru di depan dan perpustakaan yang sudah dikenal di belakang. Pilihan ketiga inversion yang aneh dan teatrikal.

material.title: Choosing the tool, and when to leave it out

id.title: Memilih alatnya, dan kapan tidak memakainya

blocks.text:
Each structure moves the spotlight in its own way. Choose the one **the text** needs:
- **Correcting an assumption → it-cleft.** *It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time.* The listener thought X; the cleft puts Y in the spotlight.
- **Building to a climax (puncak) in a speech → what-cleft or inversion, often followed by a short sentence.** *What made these twenty-five years possible wasn't a product or a strategy. It was the people in this room.* / *Never before has our team grown so fast.*
- **Contrasting two things → fronting.** *The budget we can fix; trust we can't.* (mostly spoken or in an op-ed)
- **Linking to the previous sentence, or when who did it doesn't matter → passive.** *The new system was tested in June.*
- **Sounding formal and weighty in an op-ed or report → inversion, once.** *Not only did the policy fail to cut traffic, it also raised fares.*
**When the plain order is better:** most of the time. One strong structure in a paragraph lands. Three in a row sound **theatrical** (berlebihan, seperti pidato di sinetron), especially in a LinkedIn post, an email or a chat. Inversion is never required; normal order is always correct.

id.text:
Setiap struktur memindahkan lampu sorot dengan caranya sendiri. Pilih yang dibutuhkan **teksnya**:
- **Meluruskan anggapan → it-cleft.** *It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time.* Pendengar mengira X; cleft menyorot Y.
- **Membangun puncak (klimaks) dalam pidato → what-cleft atau inversion, sering diikuti kalimat pendek.** *What made these twenty-five years possible wasn't a product or a strategy. It was the people in this room.* / *Never before has our team grown so fast.*
- **Mengontraskan dua hal → fronting.** *The budget we can fix; trust we can't.* (kebanyakan lisan atau di opini/op-ed)
- **Menyambung ke kalimat sebelumnya, atau saat pelakunya tidak penting → passive.** *The new system was tested in June.*
- **Terdengar formal dan berbobot di op-ed atau laporan → inversion, sekali saja.** *Not only did the policy fail to cut traffic, it also raised fares.*
**Kapan urutan biasa lebih baik:** hampir selalu. Satu struktur yang kuat dalam satu paragraf akan mengena. Tiga berturut-turut terdengar **teatrikal** (berlebihan, seperti pidato di sinetron), apalagi di postingan LinkedIn, email atau chat. Inversion tidak pernah wajib; urutan biasa selalu benar.

rows.en: It isn't the price that worries our clients; it's the delivery time.
rows.id: Yang membuat klien kami khawatir bukan harganya, tapi waktu pengirimannya.
rows.note: it-cleft: corrects an assumption

id.note: it-cleft: meluruskan anggapan

rows.en: What made these twenty-five years possible wasn't a product. It was the people in this room.
rows.id: Yang membuat dua puluh lima tahun ini mungkin bukanlah sebuah produk. Melainkan orang-orang di ruangan ini.
rows.note: anniversary speech: what-cleft, then a short sentence for the climax

id.note: pidato ulang tahun perusahaan: what-cleft, lalu kalimat pendek untuk puncaknya

rows.en: The budget we can fix; trust we can't.
rows.id: Anggaran bisa kita perbaiki; kepercayaan tidak.
rows.note: fronting: a sharp contrast in an op-ed

id.note: fronting: kontras yang tajam di op-ed

rows.en: Never have I felt so honoured. What I want to say is thank you. Such was your support that I cried.
rows.id: Belum pernah saya merasa sehormat ini. Yang ingin saya katakan adalah terima kasih. Saking besarnya dukungan kalian, saya sampai menangis.
rows.note: LinkedIn post: three structures in a row sound theatrical

id.note: postingan LinkedIn: tiga struktur berturut-turut terdengar teatrikal

rows.en: I'm honoured, and I want to thank you all. Your support meant more than I can say.
rows.id: Saya merasa terhormat, dan saya ingin berterima kasih kepada kalian semua. Dukungan kalian sangat berarti, lebih dari yang bisa saya ucapkan.
rows.note: the same post in plain order: warmer and more natural

id.note: postingan yang sama dengan urutan biasa: lebih hangat dan alami

blocks.text: **A quick test:** ask what the reader thinks *before* your sentence. If they believe something wrong → it-cleft. If they're waiting for the big point → what-cleft or inversion, then stop with a short sentence. If they need to know what *this* refers to → given first (often a passive). If none of these → plain order.

id.text: **Tes cepat:** tanyakan apa yang dipikirkan pembaca *sebelum* kalimatmu. Kalau mereka percaya sesuatu yang keliru → it-cleft. Kalau mereka menunggu poin besarnya → what-cleft atau inversion, lalu berhenti dengan kalimat pendek. Kalau mereka perlu tahu *ini* merujuk ke apa → yang lama di depan (sering dengan passive). Kalau tidak ada semua itu → urutan biasa.

blocks.prompt: Op-ed (practice text). Readers think the new toll road caused the traffic jams in Bandung. The writer disagrees: the jams come from the missing bus service. Which sentence makes that point best?
options: The missing bus service, not the toll road, the jams come from.
It isn't the toll road that is causing the jams; it's the missing bus service.
Never has the toll road caused the jams, but the missing bus service.
blocks.explain: Correcting what readers believe is the classic job of an it-cleft: *It isn't X that…; it's Y.* The first is a broken fronting. In the third, the inversion itself is fine, but *but the missing bus service* is an unfinished fragment and *Never* overstates the point.

id.prompt: Op-ed (teks latihan). Pembaca mengira jalan tol baru menyebabkan kemacetan di Bandung. Penulis tidak setuju: kemacetan itu datang dari tidak adanya layanan bus. Kalimat mana yang paling baik menyampaikan poin itu?
id.explain: Meluruskan apa yang dipercaya pembaca adalah tugas klasik it-cleft: *It isn't X that…; it's Y.* Pilihan pertama fronting yang rusak. Di pilihan ketiga, inversion-nya sendiri benar, tapi *but the missing bus service* adalah potongan kalimat yang tidak selesai dan *Never* melebih-lebihkan poinnya.

blocks.text:
A strong structure with a grammar slip loses all its power: the audience hears the mistake, not the point. Three slips survive even at C2:
- **Negative opener, then auxiliary + subject.** After *never, rarely, not only, little…* at the start, the auxiliary (kata kerja bantu: *have, has, do, did, is, can*…) comes **before** the subject, as in a question: ***Never have I** seen such a mess* (not *Never I have seen*). No auxiliary? Add *do / does / did* + base verb: ***Rarely do** we meet.*
- **Only when / Only after + a clause: the inversion is in the SECOND part.** *Only when I read the report **did I understand** the problem* (not *…I understood*). The first part (*when I read the report*) stays normal.
- **What-cleft: no extra it.** *What I need **is** more time* (not *What I need it is*). Indonesian *Yang saya butuhkan **adalah**…*: *adalah* = *is*, and that's all.

id.text:
Struktur yang kuat dengan satu kesalahan grammar kehilangan seluruh kekuatannya: pendengar mendengar kesalahannya, bukan poinnya. Tiga kesalahan ini masih muncul bahkan di C2:
- **Kata negatif di depan, lalu auxiliary + subjek.** Setelah *never, rarely, not only, little…* di awal kalimat, auxiliary (kata kerja bantu: *have, has, do, did, is, can*…) datang **sebelum** subjek, seperti pertanyaan: ***Never have I** seen such a mess* (bukan *Never I have seen*). Tidak ada auxiliary? Tambahkan *do / does / did* + kata kerja dasar: ***Rarely do** we meet.*
- **Only when / Only after + klausa: inversion-nya di bagian KEDUA.** *Only when I read the report **did I understand** the problem* (bukan *…I understood*). Bagian pertama (*when I read the report*) tetap normal.
- **What-cleft: tanpa it tambahan.** *What I need **is** more time* (bukan *What I need it is*). Bahasa Indonesia *Yang saya butuhkan **adalah**…*: *adalah* = *is*, cukup itu.

rows.en: Never have I seen such a mess.
rows.id: Belum pernah saya melihat kekacauan seperti ini.
rows.note: not 'Never I have seen': have jumps before I

id.note: bukan 'Never I have seen': have melompat ke depan I

rows.en: Only when I read the report did I understand the problem.
rows.id: Baru setelah membaca laporannya saya memahami masalahnya.
rows.note: the inversion is in the second part: did I understand

id.note: inversion-nya di bagian kedua: did I understand

rows.en: What I need is more time.
rows.id: Yang saya butuhkan adalah lebih banyak waktu.
rows.note: adalah = is, no extra it

id.note: adalah = is, tanpa it tambahan

rows.en: Rarely do we get feedback this honest.
rows.id: Jarang sekali kami mendapat masukan sejujur ini.
rows.note: no auxiliary in 'we get', so add do + base verb

id.note: tidak ada auxiliary di 'we get', jadi tambah do + kata kerja dasar

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** *Belum pernah **saya melihat**…*, *Baru setelah membaca laporannya **saya paham**…*: in Indonesian the order after the opener stays the same, so the English auxiliary stays behind: *Never I have seen* ✗, *Only when I read the report I understood* ✗. And *adalah* tempts an extra *it*: *What I need it is* ✗. Read your climax sentence once just for these three.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** *Belum pernah **saya melihat**…*, *Baru setelah membaca laporannya **saya paham**…*: dalam bahasa Indonesia urutan setelah kata pembukanya tetap sama, jadi auxiliary bahasa Inggrisnya ikut tertinggal: *Never I have seen* ✗, *Only when I read the report I understood* ✗. Dan *adalah* menggoda kita menambah *it*: *What I need it is* ✗. Baca kalimat puncakmu sekali lagi khusus untuk tiga hal ini.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence from a report conclusion is correct?
options: Not only the survey confirmed the problem, but it also showed its cause.
Not only did the survey confirm the problem, but it also showed its cause.
Not only did the survey confirmed the problem, but it also showed its cause.
blocks.explain: *Not only* at the start → auxiliary before the subject. *The survey confirmed* has no auxiliary, so add *did* and use the base verb: *did the survey confirm*. The first has no inversion; the third keeps the past ending after *did*.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana dari kesimpulan laporan ini yang benar?
id.explain: *Not only* di awal → auxiliary sebelum subjek. *The survey confirmed* tidak punya auxiliary, jadi tambahkan *did* dan pakai kata kerja dasar: *did the survey confirm*. Pilihan pertama tanpa inversion; pilihan ketiga masih memakai akhiran lampau setelah *did*.

id.title: Ritme: memvariasikan panjang dan struktur kalimat

blocks.text:
Correct sentences can still sound like a machine if they all have the same length and shape. Three sentence types to mix:
- **simple** = one clause (satu subjek + satu kata kerja): *Usage tripled.*
- **compound** = two main clauses joined by *and, but, so, or*: *The budget was small, but the team was strong.*
- **complex** = a main clause + a dependent clause with *when, because, although, which, if*…: *When the budget was cut, the team found cheaper suppliers.*
Four habits of good rhythm:
1. **A short sentence after long ones** lands like a punch: it's where readers stop and remember.
2. **Mix the three types**: not all simple (choppy, patah-patah), not all long (tiring).
3. **Start sentences differently**: with the subject, a time phrase (*In May, …*), a dependent clause (*Although…*), a participle clause (*Faced with these problems, …*).
4. **Read it aloud.** If you run out of breath, split a sentence. If it sounds like a list, join two.
**Practice text, before** (a report conclusion):
*We started the project in January. We interviewed forty farmers in Central Java. We found three problems. The farmers did not trust the app. The app was slow on cheap phones. The training was too short. We changed the design in May. Usage tripled.*
**After:**
*We started in January by interviewing forty farmers in Central Java, and three problems kept coming up: the farmers did not trust the app, it was slow on cheap phones, and the training was too short. In May, we redesigned the app and the training. Usage tripled.*
The facts are the same. Now there's one long, complex sentence that carries the problems, a medium one that starts differently (*In May*), and a three-word sentence at the end for punch.

id.text:
Kalimat yang benar pun bisa terdengar seperti mesin kalau semuanya sama panjang dan sama bentuknya. Tiga jenis kalimat untuk dicampur:
- **simple** (kalimat tunggal) = satu klausa (satu subjek + satu kata kerja): *Usage tripled.*
- **compound** (kalimat majemuk setara) = dua klausa utama yang disambung *and, but, so, or*: *The budget was small, but the team was strong.*
- **complex** (kalimat majemuk bertingkat) = klausa utama + anak kalimat dengan *when, because, although, which, if*…: *When the budget was cut, the team found cheaper suppliers.*
Empat kebiasaan ritme yang baik:
1. **Kalimat pendek setelah kalimat-kalimat panjang** terasa seperti pukulan: di situ pembaca berhenti dan mengingat.
2. **Campur ketiga jenisnya**: jangan semuanya pendek (patah-patah), jangan semuanya panjang (melelahkan).
3. **Mulai kalimat dengan cara berbeda**: dengan subjek, frasa waktu (*In May, …*), anak kalimat (*Although…*), participle clause (*Faced with these problems, …*).
4. **Bacakan dengan suara keras.** Kalau kamu kehabisan napas, pecah kalimatnya. Kalau terdengar seperti daftar, gabungkan dua kalimat.
**Teks latihan, sebelum** (kesimpulan laporan):
*We started the project in January. We interviewed forty farmers in Central Java. We found three problems. The farmers did not trust the app. The app was slow on cheap phones. The training was too short. We changed the design in May. Usage tripled.*
**Sesudah:**
*We started in January by interviewing forty farmers in Central Java, and three problems kept coming up: the farmers did not trust the app, it was slow on cheap phones, and the training was too short. In May, we redesigned the app and the training. Usage tripled.*
Faktanya sama. Sekarang ada satu kalimat panjang yang membawa masalah-masalahnya, satu kalimat sedang yang dimulai dengan cara berbeda (*In May*), dan kalimat tiga kata di akhir sebagai pukulan.

rows.en: Usage tripled.
rows.id: Penggunaannya naik tiga kali lipat.
rows.note: simple: a short sentence for punch after long ones

id.note: simple: kalimat pendek sebagai pukulan setelah kalimat panjang

rows.en: The budget was small, but the team was strong.
rows.id: Anggarannya kecil, tapi timnya kuat.
rows.note: compound: two main clauses joined by but

id.note: compound: dua klausa utama disambung but

rows.en: When the budget was cut, the team found cheaper suppliers.
rows.id: Ketika anggarannya dipotong, tim itu menemukan pemasok yang lebih murah.
rows.note: complex: starts with a dependent clause

id.note: complex: dimulai dengan anak kalimat

rows.en: Faced with these problems, we redesigned the app.
rows.id: Menghadapi masalah-masalah ini, kami mendesain ulang aplikasinya.
rows.note: a different opening: a participle clause

id.note: pembuka yang berbeda: participle clause

blocks.text: **Indonesian trap:** formal Indonesian (laporan, surat dinas) often chains everything into one very long sentence with *yang, dan, sehingga, serta*. Translated, that becomes a 60-word English sentence. The opposite habit, from English classes, is a row of short *We… We… We…* sentences. Good English prose **mixes** both, and the short sentence goes where you want the reader to stop.

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia formal (laporan, surat dinas) sering merangkai semuanya menjadi satu kalimat sangat panjang dengan *yang, dan, sehingga, serta*. Kalau diterjemahkan, jadinya kalimat bahasa Inggris 60 kata. Kebiasaan sebaliknya, dari kelas bahasa Inggris, adalah deretan kalimat pendek *We… We… We…*. Prosa bahasa Inggris yang baik **mencampur** keduanya, dan kalimat pendek ditaruh di tempat kamu ingin pembaca berhenti.

blocks.prompt: Report conclusion (practice text): 'Sales rose in all five regions, the new pricing reached more small shops than we expected, and our distributors in Sulawesi doubled their orders.' Which sentence works best right after it?
options: As a result of all of these positive developments in the five regions, profits also increased considerably during the period.
Profits, which followed, were also, in the end, higher.
blocks.explain: After a long sentence, a short one lands like a punch: *Profits followed.* The second is another long sentence that repeats what we know. The third is broken up by commas and loses the point.

id.prompt: Kesimpulan laporan (teks latihan): 'Sales rose in all five regions, the new pricing reached more small shops than we expected, and our distributors in Sulawesi doubled their orders.' Kalimat mana yang paling pas tepat setelahnya?
id.explain: Setelah kalimat panjang, kalimat pendek terasa seperti pukulan: *Profits followed.* Pilihan kedua kalimat panjang lagi yang mengulang hal yang sudah kita tahu. Pilihan ketiga terpotong-potong koma dan poinnya hilang.

suggestedQuestions: Is the passive always weaker than the active?
How many clefts or inversions are too many in one text?
How short can a 'punch' sentence be in a formal report?
Why does 'What I need it is' feel natural to Indonesian speakers?

flashcards.back: New or important information goes at the end: The new office opens in Surabaya in March.
Long, heavy parts go last: It surprised everyone that the ministry approved the budget without any discussion.

id.intro: Selamat datang di pelajaran grammar untuk gaya bahasa! Kamu sudah bisa membentuk cleft, inversion dan fronting. Sekarang kamu belajar memilih: di mana fokus sebuah kalimat seharusnya jatuh, struktur mana yang menaruhnya di situ dalam pidato, op-ed, laporan atau postingan LinkedIn, dan bagaimana variasi panjang kalimat memberi ritme pada tulisanmu.
suggestedQuestions: Apakah passive selalu lebih lemah daripada active?
Berapa banyak cleft atau inversion yang terlalu banyak dalam satu teks?
Seberapa pendek kalimat 'pukulan' boleh dipakai di laporan formal?
Kenapa 'What I need it is' terasa wajar bagi penutur bahasa Indonesia?

assessment.gfs-1:
Pidato pada ulang tahun ke-25 sebuah perusahaan di Bandung. Tulis auxiliary (kata kerja bantu) yang hilang.
'Rarely ___ a small family workshop grown into a company with 2,000 employees. Tonight we celebrate the people who made it happen.'
assessment.gfs-2:
Kesimpulan laporan. Tulis auxiliary (kata kerja bantu) yang hilang.
'Only when the team compared the 2023 and 2024 data ___ they notice the pattern in the complaints.'
assessment.gfs-3:
Kalimat dari postingan LinkedIn ini punya satu kata berlebih yang harus dihapus. Tulis kata itu.
'What our industry needs it is fewer meetings and more honest feedback.'
assessment.gfs-4: Kamu menulis op-ed (artikel opini) tentang banjir di Jakarta Utara. Kebanyakan pembaca mengira hujan deras adalah penyebab utamanya. Kamu ingin meluruskan anggapan itu dan menyorot tanah yang terus turun. Struktur mana dari daftar ini yang dibuat untuk tugas itu: cleft, inversion, fronting, passive? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.gfs-5:
Rapat dewan direksi. Seorang anggota dewan bertanya: 'And what's the biggest risk for the Surabaya project?'
Kamu menjawab dalam satu kalimat dengan tiga bagian ini: the biggest risk · is · the timeline.
Mengikuti end-focus, kata apa yang ada di akhir jawabanmu? Tulis kata itu.
assessment.gfs-6:
Kesimpulan laporan (teks latihan). Paragrafnya berupa deretan kalimat pendek: 'The budget was cut by 30 percent. The team still finished the project on time. The donors were impressed. …'
Gabungkan dua kalimat pertama menjadi satu kalimat complex. Tulis kata yang hilang.
'___ the budget was cut by 30 percent, the team still finished the project on time.'
assessment.gfs-7:
Kesimpulan laporan. Kalimat 1: 'In 2024 the ministry launched a reporting app for village health workers.'
Di kalimat 2 kamu ingin mulai dengan aplikasinya (sudah diketahui) dan mengakhiri dengan informasi baru: a team of four engineers from Surabaya. Struktur mana dari daftar ini yang melakukannya: cleft, inversion, fronting, passive? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
